narratives.common: Items from most groups describe the 2026 US midterms as a strong night for Democrats, with Republicans losing ground and some Senate races, notably Mississippi between Scott Colom and Cindy Hyde-Smith, and Alaska, still too close to call days later. Coverage also points to market reactions, especially in AI and tech stocks, and to questions about what the results mean for Trump and the Republican Party.

groups.distinct: Posts are personal and celebratory or activist in tone. They cite individual winners (Jon Ossoff in Georgia, Eric Armstrong in Iowa, Crystalyne Curley as the first woman elected Navajo Nation president) and a Democratic sweep of the Texas state government. Some warn that Democrats will 'betray' voters once the 'sugar high' fades, or argue the fight is to cut the party off from mega donors and the 'Israel lobby'. One post lists grievances against Trump, including Iran, Medicaid, tariffs and ICE.

Mostly local TV and professional-services outlets, with a practical and regional focus: a Nebraska 'FACT CHECK' saying there was no 'red wave', a tight North Carolina state Senate race, and Colom's lead over Hyde-Smith growing to over 2,000 votes. Law firms and consultancies (Edelman, WilmerHale) discuss implications for business, philanthropy and nonprofits, and SCOTUSblog covers the Supreme Court.

groups.distinct: Adds exit-poll and institutional angles: an AP Voter Poll explaining why Republicans lost, Mississippi's voter rolls and looming legal fights over the close Senate races, and a Louisiana Democratic 'near-miss' that raises hopes for the governor's race. Also covers Turning Point's future after Republican losses and an Anthropic IPO facing an AI backlash tied to data centers.

groups.distinct: Frames the result as a 'big 2026 wave' using charts, turnout data and Hispanic voters' role in Democratic wins. It also includes a CNN piece on 'bad news for progressive Democrats' and describes the GOP's post-election 'scramble' as pure 'Survivor'. NPR puts the tech selloff at $2 trillion, tied to fears of an AI crackdown.

groups.distinct: Highlights near-record youth turnout focused on the economy, and Native American women's historic victories alongside Trump intervening in a tight Senate race. The Lowy Institute argues Trump lost the midterms but not his hold on foreign policy, and coverage notes Trump's first post-election appearance and a JD Vance statement.

Uses stronger language such as 'midterm wipeout' and 'blue shift', and asks whether Trump's grip on his party is in doubt. It quotes Nikki Haley saying Republicans cannot blame media or academia for the loss, and adds an angle on global trust in America after 'Trumpism stumbles'.

Takes a longer-term, analytical view, looking at what the results suggest about populism and political change toward 2028 and the future of both parties. It calls the results 'historic' and gives live coverage rather than specific race details.

Focuses on Republican infighting and fallout rather than Democratic gains. It reports House Republicans erupting at Stephen Miller as Trump elevates him after the 'midterm massacre', and the 'manosphere' reaction, with Rogan saying Republicans got 'destroyed'. The WSJ also reports that Ken Paxton partied in Dubai with fugitives before the Texas Senate race.

narrative:
Discussion of the 2026 US midterms splits into five framings, with 62 of 160 items (39%) framed; the rest carry none of them. The divide is rated strong (kappa 0.6).

The largest framing is Republican and Trump fallout (35%): the defeat as a rebuke, aides questioning his focus, 2028 worries and the Iran war. Live results and vote tracking follows (29%), then markets and business (18%), voter blocs and long-term shifts (10%), and Democratic mandate and governing agenda (8%).

Outlet patterns come only from sampled headlines. CBS News, NBC News, Reuters, the Financial Times and ABC7 Bay Area each had results-tracking headlines. The Telegraph, MS NOW and The Times of India appeared mainly under Trump fallout. The Washington Post, CNBC and the Financial Times also had market or business items. WSJ had a governing-agenda item, and The Conversation had voter-bloc items. Al Jazeera appeared under both voter-bloc and Trump-fallout headlines. Among Mastodon accounts, killbait leaned toward fallout, thejapantimes toward markets, and DrALJONES toward governing agenda.

Limits: no outlet has reached the 10-item threshold and no account the 15-item threshold, so all labels are provisional. Judgments rest on headlines and snippets, and sample sizes are small.

narratives.common: A gunman opened fire in Krakow's Main Market Square in Poland, and police said five people were killed and about a dozen or more were injured. The suspect was shot by police. Early reports differed on the toll, with some outlets citing two dead and others six.

groups.distinct: Posts are mostly Polish-language reactions rather than reporting. One praises two patrol officers who pursued and 'eliminated' the attacker and says the footage is hard to watch. Others criticise the president's wording ('citizens' not 'people') and accuse TV Republika and other PiS-aligned media of politicising the tragedy. An Italian post quotes Tusk calling it a 'tragic shooting' without giving a motive. Many items are unrelated 'shooting' hashtag spam.

outlet_notes: U.S. News & World Report: center (AI estimate)
groups.distinct: Headlines stress the market-square setting and give the highest tolls, with CBS saying at least 6 dead and 15 injured. Several items are unrelated US shooting stories.

The U.S. Embassy issued a 'Security Alert' for the Main Market Square. TMZ adds that the gunman 'drove onto' the square, and a Facebook post says he was shot by police. Several items are unrelated shootings.

Sky News focuses on footage showing a police officer shooting the suspect. Hampshire Chronicle gives six dead and at least 15 injured, while the others say five dead and more than a dozen injured. Some items are unrelated UK crime stories.

groups.distinct: No comments discuss the shooting. Kraków appears only incidentally, in remarks about buses and a mislabelled photo of the Main Square.
The Guardian says the gunman fired 'at random'. The Independent's headline reports two dead, an earlier and lower figure than the other items in this group.

The distinctive item is President Zelenskyy's condemnation of the attack as a 'shocking crime'. UA.NEWS republishes The Independent's early toll of at least two dead and 10 injured, while UNITED24 reports five dead and 12 injured.

Injured count: UA.NEWS says 10 injured, UNITED24, CNBC and the Washington Post say 12, and CBS News and Hampshire Chronicle say 15.

topic: Stephen Miller named chief of staff
summary: Outlets report that Stephen Miller has been named White House chief of staff, with BBC describing Trump preparing for a battle and Miller saying he 'saved America'.

signals.name: Todd Blanche says he is Stephen Miller's lawyer
With Stephen Miller pick, Trump readies for a battle [BBC News]
Trump’s new chief of staff Stephen Miller says he ‘saved America’ [Al Jazeera]
Stephen Miller named White House Chief of Staff [France 24]

narratives.common: President Trump named Stephen Miller, previously his senior adviser and a key figure in immigration policy, as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Most outlets report the change came after Republican losses in the midterm elections.

groups.distinct: Posts are mostly personal commentary and hostile to Miller, calling him 'EVIL' and 'Lich' and calling for prosecution, removal or impeachment, and blaming him for ICE actions. One post argues Wiles was 'an enabler' and that Miller has gained no extra influence but made 'new enemies in the GOP'. Several posts are off-topic, such as a cat photo and a Politico item about a news-outlet ban.

Stresses the political fallout. Fox 5 DC reports House Republicans erupting at Miller ('Megalomaniac'), Roll Call ties the move to the coming Democratic takeover, and The Hill quotes Miller calling the post the 'honor of my life' at a Mar-a-Lago event. Headlines are mostly straightforward.

groups.distinct: Frames the appointment as a 'doubling down' on a hard-line agenda after a midterm 'rout'. Mother Jones is openly alarmed ('Hell on Earth'), while NBC, NPR and MS NOW use plain headlines.

Quotes Trump saying 'I just wanted to make a change' and presents the move as a 'fightback' ('It's Miller time'). ANI highlights Miller pledging 'absolute loyalty' and saying the US 'would not exist right now without Trump'. Open Magazine asks why Trump chose him.

Barely discusses the appointment itself. Commenters mention Miller's founding of America First Legal, with one saying 'Trump-aligned' understates it, and drift into unrelated topics such as AI and immigration.

Defines Miller by immigration enforcement, calling him the 'driving force' behind 'Operation Midway Blitz' and 'Mastermind of immigration crackdown'. ABC7 Bay Area describes him as a 'bombastic critic of Democrats' and quotes his own words. The White House (.gov) page lists him under his new title.

Presents Miller as an 'immigration hardliner' (FT) and a 'reckless' MAGA loyalist (The i Paper) through explainer-style profiles. The Economist folds the story into a news roundup next to US jobs growth.
The Guardian focuses on criticism, describing the appointment as 'dangerous' and noting the backlash it drew. The Independent runs a 'who is' profile, and HuffPost UK reports it straight.

narrative:
Coverage of Stephen Miller's naming as chief of staff splits into four framings, and the divide is rated strong (kappa 0.54). Of 160 items, 56 (35%) were framed. The largest share, 41%, is a neutral personnel announcement: Trump named Miller to replace Susie Wiles. Next is 29% tying the move to Republican midterm losses, using words like 'fires', 'blowout' and 'wipeout'. Alarm about Miller's influence makes up 16%, citing a former Trump aide who called the prospect 'terrifying'. A promotion-and-profile framing makes up 14%.

Outlet labels are tentative. CNN, Politico, CNBC, DW, WSJ, NPR, The Economist and The Washington Post show mainly neutral headlines. NDTV, The Times of India, New York Post, The Independent, The Times of Israel, AP News and Politico (one headline) show the midterm framing. NDTV, The Independent and CBS News also have profile pieces. The Times of India has one alarm-style item.

Mastodon accounts mostly use the midterm framing (alternet, elfolio, KimPerales, deadline, billykaren, both tda accounts, LiloStart) or the alarm framing (drmike, Nonilex, yourautisticlife, bazcook, scheichsbeutel). drrjv appears in both.

Limits: outlets are judged from headlines and snippets, no outlet or account has reached the item threshold, and samples are very small.
